author: Sady Swanson
title: Judge to decide if attempted murder case will move to juvenile court - NewsBreak
text:
By Sady Swanson ,
1 days ago
A judge will decide if a former Fort Collins High School student accused of breaking into a woman's apartment and physically assaulting her will continue to face charges as an adult or have his case moved into the juvenile court system.
Investigators believe Ethan Campbell, who is now 19, is the masked man who attacked a Fort Collins woman in her apartment in May 2024.
Judge Daniel McDonald ruled following a Dec. 15 evidence hearing that the prosecution had enough evidence for the case to continue toward trial. In a multiday hearing following that ruling, Campbell's defense attorneys argued that this case should be tried in juvenile court instead of adult court, which is where the case was initially filed.
Campbell was arrested in February 2025 , nearly 10 months after the woman was attacked in her home at Brookview Apartments, 1200 E. Stuart St. Campbell was 18 when he was arrested and 17 at the time of the attack.
After months of investigation without an arrest, the woman shared her story anonymously with the Coloradoan in November 2024 — detailing the assault that left her with PTSD and physical injuries that have taken away her ability to taste or smell — with hopes that someone may come forward with information on a potential suspect.
As a result, a community member did report an interaction with a man living in Brookview Apartments in January 2025, Fort Collins police said at the time of Campbell's arrest.
Fort Collins Police Services Detective Robert Tuttle said during the Dec. 15 evidence hearing that, based on a variety of leads in the case, investigators were looking for individuals matching the victim's description of the suspect who lived in the apartment complex.
Tuttle said police received a tip about a young man matching this description who had approached someone in the complex's parking lot and started asking them about religion. The person gave police the license plate of the vehicle associated with the man, which led investigators to the Campbell family and eventually Ethan Campbell.
While conducting a search warrant at Campbell's apartment, police found a black face mask with a bird face and beak depicted on it, which matched the description of the mask the victim said her attacker was wearing, Tuttle said. A retractable baton with the victim's blood on it was also found in Campbell's apartment, Tuttle said.
Investigators don't believe Campbell and the victim knew each other, Tuttle said, but they do believe Campbell may have previously approached the victim and a friend in the apartment complex's parking lot to talk about religion. The victim did not recall any previous interactions with Campbell when asked by police and shown a picture of him but did say she may have seen him walking a dog around the apartment complex, Tuttle said.
The victim told police she woke up in the early morning hours of May 4, 2024, to her dog barking, which was unusual. When she went into her living room to investigate, she saw the sliding glass door to her balcony was open.
The woman told the 911 dispatcher that a masked young man was out on her balcony and grabbed her. She said she was screaming and he told her to stop, then pushed her back into her apartment, started beating her with some type of stick and "accused me of doing something wrong," she told the dispatcher, according to a recording of the 911 call played during the Dec. 15 evidence hearing.
The woman told police he continued hitting her in the head, back and arms, and she "decided to play dead." She also believed she may have lost consciousness because she didn't see him leave but saw her dog walk back out onto the balcony. That's when she shut the sliding glass door and called 911.
The woman told police the man only stopped hitting her after she started playing dead or lost consciousness.
Campbell's defense attorney Haley Barton argued that the "degree of forced used ... doesn't rise to the level of attempted murder" because the attacker didn't make any verbal threats of killing the woman and there was no other weapon used, like a gun or stun gun. Barton also argued that "the evidence isn't there to connect Mr. Campbell to what happened."
McDonald disagreed, stating there is enough evidence to connect Campbell to the attack and that the attack was serious enough to rise to an attempted murder charge.
"There was blood all over the place," McDonald said, referencing photos and videos of the victim's apartment after the attack. "It was pretty extreme."
Campbell faces the following charges: attempted murder, a Class 2 felony; first-degree assault with a deadly weapon, a Class 3 felony; burglary, a Class 3 felony; and two violent crime sentence enhancers.
Judge to decide on if attempted murder case remains in adult court After the evidence hearing concluded, a multiday hearing to determine if this case should continue to be heard in adult court or move to juvenile court was held.
Campbell's attorneys presented expert testimony over several days to argue that the juvenile system is better equipped to rehabilitate juveniles and young adults convicted of violent crimes. Several individuals who worked with or alongside the juvenile court system testified that the juvenile system offers more mental health resources, including individual and family therapy, and other rehabilitation opportunities for those sentenced there to better prepare for their release and set them up for a more successful life long-term.
Prosecutors argued that the sentencing options in the juvenile system limit the length of the sentence someone can receive and how long they can remain under probation or parole supervision.
The victim also testified to the mental, emotional and physical toll this crime has taken on her. Injuries to her head and face have dulled her senses of smell and taste and left scars that remain a "constant reminder" of what happened to her.
"I'll never be able to get away from this," she said.
The woman said she has lost her independence and strength and is now afraid to be alone or go anywhere after dark.
"Sometimes I cry and weep and mourn this ... what I used to be and what I'm not anymore and why this happened," she said, later adding how grateful she is to know "how supported I am by the people who love me."
McDonald asked the prosecution and defense attorneys to file written arguments in January and said he would issue a written decision on whether this case will continue to be heard in adult court or move to juvenile court prior to the next court appearance, which is scheduled for Feb. 10.
All suspects are presumed innocent until proven guilty in court. Arrests and charges are merely accusations by law enforcement until, and unless, a suspect is convicted of a crime.
Reporter Erin Udell contributed to this article.
This article originally appeared on Fort Collins Coloradoan: Judge to decide if attempted murder case will move to juvenile court
